item.title: Sample Page
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
This is an example page. It's different from a blog post because it will stay in one place and will show up in your site navigation (in most themes). Most people start with an About page that introduces them to potential site visitors. It might say something like this:

Hi there! I'm a bike messenger by day, aspiring actor by night, and this is my website. I live in Los Angeles, have a great dog named Jack, and I like piña coladas. (And gettin' caught in the rain.)

...or something like this:

The XYZ Doohickey Company was founded in 1971, and has been providing quality doohickeys to the public ever since. Located in Gotham City, XYZ employs over 2,000 people and does all kinds of awesome things for the Gotham community.

As a new WordPress user, you should go to your dashboard to delete this page and create new pages for your content. Have fun!

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
Who we are

Suggested text: Our website address is: http://localhost:8888/childs/child6.

Comments

Suggested text: When visitors leave comments on the site we collect the data shown in the comments form, and also the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help spam detection.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) may be provided to the Gravatar service to see if you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After approval of your comment, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

Suggested text: If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (EXIF GPS) included. Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

Suggested text: If you leave a comment on our site you may opt-in to saving your name, email address and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you visit our login page, we will set a temporary cookie to determine if your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set up several cookies to save your login information and your screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for a year. If you select "Remember Me", your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie includes no personal data and simply indicates the post ID of the article you just edited. It expires after 1 day.

Embedded content from other websites

Suggested text: Articles on this site may include embedded content (e.g. videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in the exact same way as if the visitor has visited the other website.

These websites may collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction with the embedded content if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

Suggested text: If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long we retain your data

Suggested text: If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This is so we can recognize and approve any follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users that register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can see, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also see and edit that information.

What rights you have over your data

Suggested text: If you have an account on this site, or have left comments, you can request to receive an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided to us. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include any data we are obliged to keep for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Suggested text: Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

item.title: About me
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
PHOTOGRAPHER, ARTIST

Rosa Alexandra

I am a portrait photographer who has spent fifteen years studying faces. I've shot Fortune 500 executives, household names, and the occasional head of state — each time looking for the same thing: the moment they forget there's a camera in the room. That's when the real portrait begins.

The Eyes Behind the Lens

Based in London and Paris,Sophia is a contemporary photographer whose work explores the intersection of architectural minimalism and human emotion. With a career spanning over a decade, she has developed a signature style characterized by stark compositions, a muted tonal palette, and an unflinching focus on the subject's essence.

After graduating from the Royal College of Art, Sophia began her journey documenting the evolving urban landscapes of Europe. Her transition into fashion and portraiture allowed her to bring that same structural discipline to the human form, resulting in images that feel both grounded and ethereal. Her approach is rooted in patience—waiting for that precise nanosecond where the light, the environment, and the emotion converge.

Exhibitions & Awards

2026
LEAD PHOTOGRAPHER

Currently shooting for editorial, advertising, and corporate clients across Europe and North America. A deliberately short waiting list and a full calendar.

2025
SENIOR PORTRAIT

A defining year. Three international publication covers, a global advertising commission, and a residency at one of London's most respected portrait studios.

2023
INDEPENDENT FREELANCE

Went freelance and immediately built the client list most photographers spend a career chasing. Three international awards in the first twelve months.

item.title: People of Prague
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
People of Prague

I came to Prague in November, when the tourist crowds thin and the city settles back into itself, and I spent my mornings at tram stops, bakeries, and the edges of local markets. I chose to shoot on medium format film, which slowed me down deliberately — each frame cost something, so I only pressed the shutter when I was certain. The cold light of Central European autumn gave every portrait a quiet, interior quality that I hadn't planned for but came to love. Prague gave me people who were guarded at first and generous once they understood what I was trying to do.

item.title: Still Here
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
Still Here

This series began as an experiment in stripping everything away — no location, no story, no context beyond what a person carries in their face. I worked with a single large softbox and a seamless white background, keeping the setup identical for every session so that the only variable was the subject. Each sitting lasted about two hours, long enough for the initial self-consciousness to dissolve and something more unguarded to come through. What I was looking for, and what I think I found in some of these frames, is the expression that exists in the space between poses — unheld, unperformed.

item.title: People of Tbilisi
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
People of Tbilisi

Walking through Tbilisi's tangled old town, I spent three weeks approaching strangers in courtyards, markets, and tea houses, asking if I could photograph them where they stood. I worked entirely with natural light — the city's golden afternoon sun and the deep shadow of its narrow balconied streets became my studio. Most of my subjects spoke no English and I spoke no Georgian, so everything was communicated through gesture, patience, and the moment someone finally relaxed and forgot about the camera. What emerged was a portrait of a city that feels both ancient and restless, carried in the faces of the people who call it home.

item.title: minimalio
item.dc:creator: Minimalio

item.title: The Portrait That Almost Didn't Happen
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
There's a photograph in my Prague series that I nearly didn't make. It was late in the trip, the last week of a month I'd spent in the city, and I was tired in the way that sets in near the end of long projects — tired of looking, tired of asking, tired of not speaking the language. I almost didn't go out that morning. I made coffee, sat by the window of the apartment I'd rented in Žižkov, watched trams go past, and eventually put on my coat more out of habit than intention.

I ended up at a small indoor market near Náměstí Míru, the kind of place that sells pickles and dried mushrooms and seasonal vegetables in wooden crates. There was a man there, perhaps seventy, working behind a counter covered in jars. He had the face of someone who had been in that market for a very long time — settled into it, almost architectural. I watched him for a while from across the room, buying things I didn't need so I had a reason to stay.

Eventually I walked up to his counter and pointed at my camera and then at him, the universal gesture, ready to be refused. He looked at me for a long moment, then at the camera, then back at me. He said something in Czech I didn't understand and gestured at the space behind his counter. I walked around, stood where he'd indicated, and he arranged himself with a kind of practiced dignity that suggested he had been photographed before and knew exactly how he wanted to look. I shot six frames. He shook my hand. I left.

I've thought about that morning a lot, particularly about how close I came to staying in the apartment. The photograph exists because I put my coat on when I didn't feel like it, walked somewhere without a plan, and waited long enough for something to happen. Most of the best travel portraits I've made have come about this way — not through technique or preparation but through simple persistence. The discipline of continuing to show up, especially when you don't feel like it, is the closest thing to a method I've found that actually works.

item.title: On Shooting Film in Cities
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
There is a particular discipline that comes from traveling with a finite number of frames. I started shooting medium format film seriously about four years ago, initially because I liked the image quality, and later because of what the limitations did to my decision-making in the field. When you have twelve frames on a roll and you're walking through a city you don't know, you become selective in a way that's hard to manufacture artificially.

I was in Lisbon for six weeks working on a street portrait project, carrying two film cameras and nothing else. I'd load a roll in the morning, go out, and sometimes come back in the evening having shot nothing — not because nothing happened, but because nothing happened that I was willing to spend a frame on. That sounds wasteful, and by some measures it is. But it changed how I looked. I stopped scanning for photographs and started paying attention to the city itself, and paradoxically that's when the photographs appeared.

Film also changes the relationship with your subjects, in ways I didn't expect. There's a sound, a weight, a visible deliberateness to shooting on a medium format camera that makes the act of photographing someone feel like a declaration rather than a reflex. People notice. They take a breath. Some of them straighten up, some of them soften. The camera becomes a shared object rather than something I'm pointing at them, and that shift in the social dynamic shows up in the images.

The practical challenges are real. Film is expensive, especially when you're traveling. Labs can be unreliable. You can't check the back of the camera to see what you got. I've lost rolls to airport X-rays and had development errors ruin work I couldn't go back for. But these difficulties have also made me less precious about individual images — if something is lost, it's lost, and the only response is to go back out and shoot more. That attitude, which film forced on me, has ended up being one of the more useful things I've learned as a photographer.

item.title: What Strangers Taught Me
item.dc:creator: Minimalio
item.content:encoded:
I used to think portrait photography was about technical control: the right focal length, the right light ratio, the right moment. I spent years refining those things, and they matter. But the most useful lesson I've learned as a photographer who works primarily on the road — in cities I don't know, in languages I don't speak — is that the camera is almost beside the point. What actually determines whether a portrait is alive or dead is everything that happened before you raised it to your eye.

I first understood this in Tbilisi, during a period when I was shooting on the streets for a project I had no real plan for. I had my camera with me the way you carry keys — always there, rarely thought about. One afternoon I sat for almost an hour on a low wall outside a bread bakery in the old town, not photographing anything, just watching. A woman came out to sweep the step. We nodded at each other. Twenty minutes later she came back out with two small cups of tea and handed me one. I photographed her after that, in the doorway, in maybe four frames. Those four frames are some of the best work I've made.

What the tea taught me is that presence comes before the picture. When you arrive somewhere trying to take photographs, people feel it immediately — there is something extractive about that intention, and it shows in the images. When you arrive somewhere trying to understand it, the photographs come as a consequence of actually being there. This sounds obvious when written down, and I have read variations of it in every photography book I've ever owned, but I needed to learn it slowly, in actual places, with actual people who had no reason to trust me.

Traveling to make portraits has also changed my relationship with time. I used to move fast, covering ground, producing volume. Now I try to stay in a neighborhood long enough that I become boring — long enough that people stop noticing me, or start expecting me. That familiarity is where the good work lives. You can't rush it, and you can't fake it with a more expensive camera. You just have to be there, and keep being there, until the place lets you in.
